nodes.statement: item Fourier measure of partial smoothing effect of T: In Crefsec:ill_posedness, we introduce a new framework based on Fourier spectra which quantifies the partial smoothing effect of T for functions f:XtimesOtoR with only high frequencies on X; while conversely quantifies the partial anti-smoothing effect of T for functions f:XtimesOtoR with only low frequencies on X. Our Fourier measure of partial smoothing effect resembles existing ones based on sieves~citepblundell2007semi,chen2024adaptiveestimationuniformconfidence,kim2025optimality, but features two key distinctions: 1) Our framework takes into account the partial identity structure of T caused by the existence of observed covariates O. 2) Our framework aligns, through Bochner's theorem, with the RKHS of a continuous translational invariant kernel. This alignment will be useful for our next contribution.
nodes.raw_latex:
\item \emph{Fourier measure of partial smoothing effect of $T$}:
    In \Cref{sec:ill_posedness}, we introduce a new framework based on Fourier spectra which quantifies the \emph{partial} smoothing effect of $T$ for functions $f:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{O}\to\mathbb{R}$ with only high frequencies on $X$; while conversely quantifies the \emph{partial} anti-smoothing effect of $T$ for functions $f:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{O}\to\mathbb{R}$ with only low frequencies on $X$. 
    Our Fourier measure of partial smoothing effect resembles existing ones based on sieves~\citep{blundell2007semi,chen2024adaptiveestimationuniformconfidence,kim2025optimality}, but features two key distinctions:
    1) Our framework takes into account the partial identity structure of $T$ caused by the existence of observed covariates $O$.
    2) Our framework aligns, through Bochner's theorem, with the RKHS of a continuous translational invariant kernel. This alignment will be useful for our next contribution.
nodes.clean_text: item Fourier measure of partial smoothing effect of T: In Crefsec:ill_posedness, we introduce a new framework based on Fourier spectra which quantifies the partial smoothing effect of T for functions f:XtimesOtoR with only high frequencies on X; while conversely quantifies the partial anti-smoothing effect of T for functions f:XtimesOtoR with only low frequencies on X. Our Fourier measure of partial smoothing effect resembles existing ones based on sieves~citepblundell2007semi,chen2024adaptiveestimationuniformconfidence,kim2025optimality, but features two key distinctions: 1) Our framework takes into account the partial identity structure of T caused by the existence of observed covariates O. 2) Our framework aligns, through Bochner's theorem, with the RKHS of a continuous translational invariant kernel. This alignment will be useful for our next contribution.

nodes.statement: item Upper and minimax lower L^2(P_XO)-learning rate: Under the above framework that quantifies the partial smoothing effect of T, we prove an upper learning rate (Crefthm:upper_rate) for a kernel based algorithm for instrumental variable regression with observed covariates proposed in citetsingh2024kernel, termed KIV-O. Furthermore, we prove the first minimax lower learning rate (Crefthm:lower_rate) for NPIV-O defined in Eq.~. All our bounds hold in the strong L^2(P_XO) norm rather than the pseudo-metric \|T(cdot)\|_L^2(P_ZO) considered in citetsingh2019kernel. For the following two edge cases: 1) No observed covariates: NPIV-O reduces to classical NPIV; 2) No hidden confounding: instrument variables Z are unnecessary and NPIV-O reduces to NPR, our upper bound of KIV-O matches the minimax lower bound, recovering earlier results on minimax optimality of classical kernel instrumental variable regression~citepmeunier2024nonparametricinstrumentalregressionkernel and kernel ridge regression~citephang2021optimal,fischer2020sobolev, respectively established under analogous assumptions to our work. In the general intermediate case stevewhere T exhibits a partial identity structure, both our upper and lower learning rates interpolate accordingly, however, there exists a gap between the upper and minimax lower bound. steveWe posit that this gap is fundamental and we provide insights on why this gap emerges in Crefsec:challenge_optimal.
nodes.raw_latex:
\item \emph{Upper and minimax lower $L^2(P_{XO})$-learning rate}: 
    Under the above framework that quantifies the \emph{partial} smoothing effect of $T$, we prove an upper learning rate (\Cref{thm:upper_rate}) for a kernel based algorithm for instrumental variable
    regression with observed covariates proposed in \citet{singh2024kernel}, termed KIV-O. Furthermore, we prove the first minimax lower learning rate (\Cref{thm:lower_rate}) for NPIV-O defined in Eq.~\eqref{eq:npiv_o_intro}. All our bounds hold in the strong $L^2(P_{XO})$ norm rather than the pseudo-metric $\|T(\cdot)\|_{L^2(P_{ZO})}$ considered in \citet{singh2019kernel}. 
    For the following two edge cases: 1)
    No observed covariates: NPIV-O reduces to classical NPIV; 2) No hidden confounding: instrument variables $Z$ are unnecessary and NPIV-O reduces to NPR, our upper bound of KIV-O matches the minimax lower bound, recovering earlier results on minimax optimality of classical kernel instrumental variable regression~\citep{meunier2024nonparametricinstrumentalregressionkernel} and kernel ridge regression~\citep{hang2021optimal,fischer2020sobolev}, respectively established under analogous assumptions to our work. In the general intermediate case \steve{where $T$ exhibits a partial identity structure}, both our upper and lower learning rates interpolate accordingly, however, there exists a gap between the upper and minimax lower bound. \steve{We posit that this gap is fundamental and we provide insights on why this gap emerges in \Cref{sec:challenge_optimal}.

Furthermore, we prove the first minimax lower learning rate (Crefthm:lower_rate) for NPIV-O defined in Eq.~. All our bounds hold in the strong L^2(P_XO) norm rather than the pseudo-metric \|T(cdot)\|_L^2(P_ZO) considered in citetsingh2019kernel. For the following two edge cases: 1) No observed covariates: NPIV-O reduces to classical NPIV; 2) No hidden confounding: instrument variables Z are unnecessary and NPIV-O reduces to NPR, our upper bound of KIV-O matches the minimax lower bound, recovering earlier results on minimax optimality of classical kernel instrumental variable regression~citepmeunier2024nonparametricinstrumentalregressionkernel and kernel ridge regression~citephang2021optimal,fischer2020sobolev, respectively established under analogous assumptions to our work. In the general intermediate case stevewhere T exhibits a partial identity structure, both our upper and lower learning rates interpolate accordingly, however, there exists a gap between the upper and minimax lower bound. steveWe posit that this gap is fundamental and we provide insights on why this gap emerges in Crefsec:challenge_optimal.

nodes.statement: item Interpretable anisotropic smoothness assumption: Another key feature of our upper and lower bounds is that they highlight the separate contribution of the partial smoothing effect of T and the anisotropic smoothness of f_ast, characterized by an anisotropic Besov space. In contrast, much work in the NPIV literature employ a generalized source condition with respect to the unknown conditional expectation operator T citepengl1996regularization, singh2019kernel, mastouri2021proximal, singh2023kernel, bozkurt2025densityratiobasedproxycausal,HallHorowitz2005, which is less interpretable because T is unknown a priori and cannot reveal the separate contribution of the intrinsic (anisotropic) smoothness of f_ast and the smoothness of T.
nodes.raw_latex:
\item \emph{Interpretable anisotropic smoothness assumption}: 
    Another key feature of our upper and lower bounds is that they highlight the separate contribution of the partial smoothing effect of $T$ and the anisotropic smoothness of $f_{\ast}$, characterized by an anisotropic Besov space. 
    In contrast, much work in the NPIV literature employ a generalized source condition with respect to the unknown conditional expectation operator $T$ \citep{engl1996regularization, singh2019kernel, mastouri2021proximal, singh2023kernel, bozkurt2025densityratiobasedproxycausal,HallHorowitz2005}, which is less interpretable because $T$ is unknown a priori and cannot reveal the separate contribution of the intrinsic (anisotropic) smoothness of $f_{\ast}$ and the smoothness of $T$.

nodes.statement: Every RKHS H has a unique symmetric, positive definite reproducing kernel k : Xtimes Xto R, which satisfies k(mathbf x,cdot)in H for all mathbf xin X and langle f, k(cdot, mathbf x)rangle_H = f(mathbf x) for all fin H and mathbf xin X (the reproducing property).

nodes.statement: steveWe let k_Z and k_O, 1 be any positive definite kernels such that their associated RKHSs steveH_Z, H_O,1 are steverespectively norm equivalent to real-valued Sobolev spaces W_2^t_z(Z) and W_2^t_o(O), where t_z > fracd_z2,t_o > fracd_o2. Following , we say that k_Z, k_O, 1 are Sobolev reproducing kernels of smoothness t_z, t_o. An important example of Sobolev reproducing kernel is the Matérn-nu kernel whose RKHS is norm equivalent to a Sobolev space W^t_2 of smoothness t = nu+d/2~citep[Corollary 10.48]wendland2004scattered. Since all Sobolev reproducing kernels are bounded and measurable, k_Z, k_O,1 satisfy Crefass: kernel_technical. With the above choice of k_Z and k_O,1, it follows from Creflem:equivalence_G that the vector-valued RKHS G associated with the operator-valued kernel in Eq.~ is norm equivalent to the mixed-smoothness Sobolev space MW^t_z,t_o(ZtimesO;H_X). Since F_ast in MW^m_z,m_o_2(ZtimesO;H_X) as established above, F_ast lies in the appropriate power space of G for suitably chosen (t_z,t_o). Consequently, citetlietal2022optimal,meunier2024optimalratesvectorvaluedspectral show that estimating the CME via Eq.~ achieves the minimax-optimal rate in both the L^2(ZtimesO;H_X) and G norms, provided that the regularization parameter xi is selected adaptively with respect to the sample size tilden.

An important example of Sobolev reproducing kernel is the Matérn-$\nu$ kernel whose RKHS is norm equivalent to a Sobolev space $W^{t}_2$ of smoothness $t = \nu+d/2$~\citep[Corollary 10.48]{wendland2004scattered}. \label{rem:kernel_stage_2_choice}
We choose $k_X$ and $k_{O,2}$ to be Gaussian kernels $k_{\gamma_x}$ and $k_{\gamma_o}$ with bandwidths $\gamma_x\in (0,1), \gamma_o\in (0,1)$.
Denote $\mathcal{H}_{\gamma_x}$ and $\mathcal{H}_{\gamma_o}$ as the associated Gaussian RKHSs; $\phi_{\gamma_x}$ and $\phi_{\gamma_o}$ as the associated feature maps. 
The tensor product RKHS $\mathcal{H}_{\gamma_x,\gamma_o} := \mathcal{H}_{\gamma_x} \otimes \mathcal{H}_{\gamma_o}$ is the unique RKHS associated with the product kernel
\begin{talign}\label{eq:anis_gaussian_kernel}
    k_{\gamma_x}(\mathbf x,\mathbf x') \cdot k_{\gamma_o}(\mathbf o,\mathbf o') = \exp\left(-\sum_{j=1}^{d_x}\frac{(x_j - x_j')^2}{\gamma_x^2} - \sum_{j=1}^{d_o}\frac{(o_j - o_j')^2}{\gamma_o^2}\right).
\end{talign}
This kernel is called an anisotropic Gaussian kernel and its associated RKHS $\mathcal{H}_{\gamma_x,\gamma_o}$ is the corresponding anisotropic Gaussian RKHS. 
\citet{hang2021optimal} proves that kernel ridge regression with anisotropic Gaussian kernel in the form of Eq.~\eqref{eq:anis_gaussian_kernel} is minimax optimal for anisotropic Besov space target functions, provided that both the regularization parameter and the kernel lengthscale $\gamma_x, \gamma_o$ are \emph{adaptive} to the number of samples $n$. 
Such adaptivity will also be evident in our setting (see \Cref{thm:upper_rate}).
\citet{singh2019kernel} adopt the median heuristic for selecting the kernel lengthscale in KIV algorithm, a widely used practical choice. Unlike ours, however, the theoretical relationship between their heuristic and the underlying smoothness of the target function remains unclear.

nodes.name: Why use different kernels in Stage I and Stage II
nodes.statement: We briefly explain the rationale for selecting different types of kernels for Stage I and Stage II. For Stage I, the regression target is the conditional mean embedding F_ast. By Crefassn: technical, we have shown that F_ast belongs to the mixed Sobolev space MW^m_z,m_o(ZtimesO;H), which can be learned at the minimax optimal rate using a tensor-product Sobolev RKHS (see Crefprop:cme_rate). On the other hand, the Stage II regression target f_ast belongs to an anisotropic Besov space (Crefass:f_ast). citethang2021optimal has proved that learning an anisotropic function in a nonparametric regression setting is minimax optimal via an anisotropic Gaussian RKHS. We have followed their approach with additional refinements to our setting, that reveals the interplay between the effect of T and the anisotropic smoothness of f_ast. See Crefsec:theory for the details.

We briefly explain the rationale for selecting different types of kernels for Stage I and Stage II.

By \Cref{assn: technical}, we have shown that $F_{\ast}$ belongs to the mixed Sobolev space $MW^{m_z,m_o}(\mathcal{Z}\times\mathcal{O};\mathcal{H})$, which can be learned at the minimax optimal rate using a tensor-product Sobolev RKHS (see \Cref{prop:cme_rate}).

\citet{hang2021optimal} has proved that learning an anisotropic function in a nonparametric regression setting is minimax optimal via an anisotropic Gaussian RKHS. 
We have followed their approach with additional refinements to our setting, that reveals the interplay between the effect of $T$ and the anisotropic smoothness of $f_{\ast}$. See \Cref{sec:theory} for the details.

nodes.name: Connection with sieve measure of ill-posedness
nodes.statement: In this remark, we connect Crefass:T_frequency_ill_posedness to the sieve measure of ill-posedness condition employed in the analysis of sieve 2SLS~citepblundell2007semi, Chen_2018, chen2024adaptiveestimationuniformconfidence,kim2025optimality. For this remark, we omit observed covariates O, and take T : L^2(P_X)to L^2(P_Z). The sieve measure of ill-posedness is defined as tau_J^sieve := sup_0neq fin Psi_J frac\|f\|_L^2(P_X)\|Tf\|_L^2(P_Z), where Psi_J denotes the Jth sieve space for the treatment variable citep[Section 3]Chen_2018. For this remark, we let Psi_J be the linear span of cardinal B-splines of order m up to resolution K with J = (2^K + m + 1)^d_x asymp 2^Kd_x citep[Section 5]devore1993constructive. We note that the parameter gamma^-1, where gamma occurs in the definition of the function space LF(gamma) in Eq. , plays a role analogous to the resolution level K for cardinal B-splines. Indeed, LF(gamma) for smaller values of gamma (or Psi_J for larger values of J) correspond to a class of less smooth functions. The above observation and the form of Eq. thus suggests an analogous definition: tau_gamma^Fourier := sup_0neq fin LF(gamma)cap L^infty(P_XO) frac\|f\|_L^2(P_X)\|Tf\|_L^2(P_Z). We can thus restate Crefass:T_frequency_ill_posedness as: there exists a constant c_0>0 and a parameter eta_0in [0,infty) depending only on T, such that for all gammain (0,1), the following inequality is satisfied: tau_gamma^Fourierleq c_0^-1gamma^-d_xeta_0. In the sieve NPIV literature citepblundell2007semi,chen2024adaptiveestimationuniformconfidence, Chen_2018, an NPIV model is said to be mildly ill-posed if tau_J^sieve = O(J^eta) = O(2^etaKd_x). By the analogy between tau_gamma^Fourier and tau_J^sieve, we see that our Crefass:T_frequency_ill_posedness characterizes a mildly ill-posed regime.

nodes.name: Existing treatment of partial smoothing of $T$ in NPIV-O
nodes.statement: Existing work that concerns NPIV-O in the literature circumvents the partial identity structure of T either by imposing additional structural assumptions~citepblundell2007semi, syrgkanis2019machine or by stratifying the problem on O~citephorowitz2011applied thereby reducing NPIV-O to NPIV, which is statistically inefficient and scales poorly with the dimension of O. Instead of T, citet[Section 3.3]Chen_2018 consider the compactness and the smoothing effect of the partial conditional expectation operator T_mathbf o: L^2(P_Xmid O = mathbf o)to L^2(P_Zmid O=mathbf o) for each mathbf oin O . citet[Section 3.3]Chen_2018 proves that, if Psi_J (defined in the above remark) equals the span of the first J eigenvectors of T_mathbf o^ast T_mathbf o for any mathbf oinO, then tau_J^sieve asymp E_mathbf osim O[mu_J, mathbf o^2]^-frac12, where mu_J,mathbf o is the Jth singular value of T_mathbf o arranged in non-increasing order. citetChen_2018 then claims that the convergence rates derived for the standard NPIV can be extended to NPIV-O. However, we identify an essential oversight: citet[Assumption 4 (ii)]Chen_2018, which is required for their L^2-norm upper bound, cannot hold in the NPIV-O setting. This assumption states that for Psi_J, f_ast satisfies the following inequality: tau_J^sieve\|T(f_ast - Pi_J f_ast)\|_L^2(P_ZO)leq \|f_ast - Pi_Jf_ast\|_L^2(P_XO), where Pi_J: L^2(P_XO)to Psi_J denotes the L^2-orthogonal projection from L^2(P_XO) onto Psi_J. In the NPIV-O setting, if f_ast depends only on mathbf o and P_XO is the Lebesgue measure, then the projection Pi_J f_ast also depends only on mathbf o. This implies (T^ast T)(f_ast - Pi_J f_ast) = f_ast - Pi_J f_ast as per Eq.~, forcing tau_J^sieve^-1 = O(1), causing a contradiction with the measure of ill-posedness condition that tau_J^sieve = O(J^eta_0) unless eta_0 = 0. citetHallHorowitz2005 addresses NPIV-O by assuming smoothness of f_ast(cdot, mathbf o) relative to R(T_mathbf o^ast T_mathbf o) for each mathbf oinO, which is hard to interpret because T_mathbf o is unknown in NPIV-O.

nodes.name: Gaussian kernel ridge regression with Besov space target functions
nodes.statement: To establish learning rates for kernel ridge regression, there are two main techniques in the literature: the empirical process technique~citepsteinwart2008support,steinwart2009optimal and the integral operator technique~citepfischer2020sobolev,Lin_2020,smale2007learning,caponnetto2007optimal,blanchard2018optimal. Previous works on Gaussian kernel ridge regression with Besov space targets~citepeberts2013optimal, hang2021optimal,hamm2021adaptive rely on an oracle inequality proved via empirical process techniques~citep[Theorem 7.23]steinwart2008support, which necessitates a clipping operation on the estimator. On the other hand, the integral operator technique avoids the clipping operation, but it requires the target f_ast in a power space of the RKHS---a condition known as the source condition~citep[SRC]fischer2020sobolev---which does not hold for Besov space targets and Gaussian RKHSs. In our proof in step 2, we prove an upper learning rate of Gaussian kernel ridge regression with Besov space target functions without clipping the estimator. Specifically, we combine the two techniques above, in that we bound the approximation error with citethang2021optimal, while we bound the estimation error with the integral operator technique~citepfischer2020sobolev. To be precise, define f_lambda := arg\,min_fin H_gamma_x,gamma_olambda\|f\|^2_H_gamma_x,gamma_o + \|T([f] - f_ast)\|^2_L^2(P_ZO). The learning risk \|T([barf_lambda] - f_ast) \|_L^2(P_ZO) can be decomposed into an estimation error term \|T([barf_lambda] - [f_lambda])\|_L^2(P_ZO) and an approximation error term \|T([f_lambda] - f_ast)\|_L^2(P_ZO). We upper bound the estimation error with citet[Theorem 16]fischer2020sobolev, once we prove that the RKHS H_FO satisfies an embedding property (see citet[EMB]fischer2020sobolev), which avoids the clipping operation. We upper bound the approximation error with citet[Theorem 4]hang2021optimal, which avoids the source condition.

nodes.name: Extension to more anisotropy
nodes.statement: For simplicity of presentation, we focus on the case where anisotropic smoothness exists across (X,O) but we assume no anisotropy within X and O. The KIV-O algorithm with adaptive length-scales and its associated learning rate can both be easily extended to the fully anisotropic setting, where f_ast in B_2, infty^boldsymbols (XtimesO) with boldsymbols=[s_1, ldots, s_d_x, s_d_x+1, ldots, s_d_x+d_o]inR^d_x+d_o, a generalization of previous results from anisotropic nonparametric regression~citephang2021optimal, suzuki2021deep,hoffman2002random to anisotropic NPIV-O. This is particularly relevant in applied work, where the observed covariates O are often of high dimensionality, because practitioners tend to adjust for as many observed covariates as possible to mitigate unobserved confounding. In such cases, our KIV-O algorithm with adaptive length-scales adapts to the intrinsic smoothness with respect to O. This mitigates the slow rates typically caused by a high ambient dimension when the intrinsic smoothness is high, as our learning rates avoid being limited by the worst-case smoothness across all dimensions.

nodes.name: Comparison to existing $L^2$-minimax lower bounds for NPIV regression
nodes.statement: The work citetchen2011rate established minimax rate-optimality in L^2-norm for NPIV under an approximation condition and link condition. For a conveniently chosen compact operator B, the approximation condition characterizes the smoothness of the structural function by the optimal L^2-rate approximation by the eigenvectors of B, and the link condition relates the mapping properties of the conditional expectation operator T to the Hilbert scale generated by B. This framework subsumes an earlier minimax convergence rate result in citetHallHorowitz2005, and was subsequently instantiated in citetChen_2018 for a B constructed via a wavelet basis, and generalized to kernel instrumental variables in citetmeunier2024nonparametricinstrumentalregressionkernel with a Hilbert scale given by the covariance operator of the RKHS. A crucial limitation of this framework is the link condition can only hold if the singular values of the conditional expectation operator are decaying to zero. Thus the minimax framework given by the link condition is applicable only when T is compact, and is not suitable for our observed covariates setting.

A crucial limitation of this framework is the link condition can only hold if the singular values of the conditional expectation operator are decaying to zero. Thus the minimax framework given by the link condition is applicable only when $T$ is compact, and is not suitable for our observed covariates setting.

\label{defi:ani_b_spliine_main}
The cardinal B-spline of order $\mathfrak{m}\in \mathbb{N}$ is defined as the repeated $\mathfrak{m}$ times convolution $\iota_{\mathfrak{m}} = \iota_{0}\ast \dots \ast \iota_0$ where $\iota_0$ is the indicator function $\mathbbm{1}_{[0,1]}$. Let $d$ denote the ambient dimension, and let $\boldsymbol{s} = (s_1,\dots, s_d)$ denote a smoothness vector. Define the notation $\underline{s} = \min(s_1,\dots,s_{d})$ and $s_i^\prime := \frac{\underline{s}}{s_i}$ for $1\leq i\leq d$.  The (anisotropic) B-spline  of order $\mathfrak{m}$ with resolution $\mathfrak{K} \in \mathbb{N}_+$ and location vector $ {\boldsymbol\ell} \in  \prod_{i=1}^{d}\{-\mathfrak{m},-\mathfrak{m}+1,\dots, 2^{\left\lfloor \mathfrak{K} s_i^\prime \right\rfloor} \}$ is defined as $M_{\mathfrak{K},{\boldsymbol\ell}}(\mathbf x) = \prod_{i=1}^{d} \iota_{\mathfrak{m}} (2^{\lfloor \mathfrak{K} s_i^\prime \rfloor}x_i - \ell_i)$.

We have f_gamma,epsilonin LFleft((gamma^-1 + epsilon)^-1right)cap HF(gamma)cap L^infty(P_XO). We define the translation of a distribution $u\in \mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ via $\tau_{\mathbf z}u[\phi] = u[\tau_{-\mathbf z}\phi]$

nodes.statement: Fix igeq 1. For a Hilbert space H, B_H denotes the unit ball in H, and B(x, r, \|cdot \|_H) denotes the ball in H centred at xinH with radius r. Fix epsilon>0 such that exists g_1, dots, g_2^i-1 in B_H_gamma_x,gamma_o such that B_H_gamma_x,gamma_o subseteq bigcup_i=1^2^i-1Bleft(g_i, epsilon, \|cdot \|_L^2(P_XO)right). Fix fin B_H_FO and an arbitrary tildeepsilon>0. By citet[Eq. (4.11)]steinwart2008support, there exists gin H_gamma_x,gamma_o such that f = langle g, F_ast(cdot, cdot)otimes phi_gamma_o(cdot)rangle_H_gamma_x,gamma_o = Vg, and \|g\|_H_gamma_x,gamma_oleq 1 + tildeepsilon. By the preceding statement, (exists iin \1,dots, 2^i-1\) such that \|g - (1+tildeepsilon)g_i\|_L^2(P_XO)leq epsilon(1 + tildeepsilon). For iin \1,dots, 2^i-1\, define f_i = (1+tildeepsilon)Vg_i = (1+tildeepsilon)langle g_i, F_ast(cdot, cdot)otimes phi_gamma_o(cdot)rangle_H_gamma_x,gamma_o. Then we have \|f - f_i\|^2_L^2(P_ZO) &= int_Ztimes Olangle g - (1+tildeepsilon)g_i, F_ast(mathbf z,mathbf o)otimes phi_gamma_o(mathbf o)rangle_H_gamma_x,gamma_o^2p(mathbf z,mathbf o)\;dmathbf z\;dmathbf o\\ &= int_Ztimes OE[(g-(1+tildeepsilon)g_i)(X,O)mid Z = mathbf z,O = mathbf o]^2p(mathbf z,mathbf o)\;dmathbf z\;dmathbf o\\ &leq \|g - (1+tildeepsilon) g_i\|^2_L^2(P_XO), where the inequality is deduced by Jensen's inequality. We find thus that H_B_FOsubseteq bigcup_i=1^2^i-1B(f_i, epsilon(1+tildeepsilon), \|cdot\|_L^2(P_ZO)). Hence e_i(id: H_FOhookrightarrow L^2(P_ZO)) leq epsilon(1+tildeepsilon). Since epsilon > e_i(id:H_gamma_x,gamma_ohookrightarrow L^2(P_XO)) and tildeepsilon>0 are arbitrary, it follows that e_i(id:H_FOhookrightarrow L^2(P_ZO))leq e_i(id:H_gamma_x,gamma_ohookrightarrow L^2(P_XO)).

nodes.name: Continuous embedding
nodes.statement: A Hilbert space (X,\|cdot\|) is said to continuously embed into Hilbert space (Y,\|cdot\|) if Xsubset Y and there exists a constant C such that \|x\|_Yleq C\|x\|_X for all xin X. We denote this as Xhookrightarrow Y. The embedding norm \|Xhookrightarrow Y\| is defined as the smallest constant C for which the above inequality holds.

    \stackrel{(b)}{=}& \int_{\mathcal{Z}}\int_{\mathcal{O}}\left(\sum_{\boldsymbol\beta_1+\boldsymbol\beta_2 = \boldsymbol\beta}\binom{\boldsymbol\beta}{\boldsymbol\beta_1}\int_{\mathcal{X}} \partial^{\boldsymbol\beta_1}_{\mathbf o} w(\mathbf x,\mathbf o) \partial^{\boldsymbol\alpha}_{\mathbf z}\partial^{\boldsymbol\beta_2}_{\mathbf o}p(\mathbf x\mid \mathbf z,\mathbf o)\;\mathrm{d}\mathbf x\right)^2\;\mathrm{d}\mathbf z\;\mathrm{d}\mathbf o\\
    \stackrel{(c)}{\leq}& \int_{\mathcal{Z}}\int_{\mathcal{O}}\left(\sum_{\boldsymbol\beta_1+\boldsymbol\beta_2 = \boldsymbol\beta}\binom{\boldsymbol\beta}{\boldsymbol\beta_1}\left(\int_{\mathcal{X}} \left(\partial^{\boldsymbol\beta_1}_{\mathbf o} w(\mathbf x,\mathbf o) \right)^2\;\mathrm{d}\mathbf x\right)^{\frac{1}{2}} \left(\int_{\mathcal{X}} \left(\partial^{\boldsymbol\alpha}_{\mathbf z}\partial^{\boldsymbol\beta_2}_{\mathbf o}p(\mathbf x\mid \mathbf z,\mathbf o)\right)^2 \;\mathrm{d}\mathbf x\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\right)^2\;\mathrm{d}\mathbf z\;\mathrm{d}\mathbf o\\
    \leq & \left(\sum_{\boldsymbol\beta_1+\boldsymbol\beta_2 = \beta}\binom{\boldsymbol\beta}{\boldsymbol\beta_1}\right)^2 \left(\max_{\boldsymbol\beta_2\leq \beta}\sup_{\mathbf x,\mathbf z,\mathbf o}\left|\partial^{\boldsymbol\alpha}_{\mathbf z}\partial^{\boldsymbol\beta_2}_{\mathbf o}p(\mathbf x\mid \mathbf z,\mathbf o)\right|^2\right) \int_{\mathcal{Z}}\int_{\mathcal{O}} \max_{\boldsymbol\beta_1\leq \beta} \int_{\mathcal{X}}\left(\partial^{\boldsymbol\beta_1}_{\mathbf o}w(\mathbf x,\mathbf o)\right)^2\;\mathrm{d}\mathbf x \;\mathrm{d}\mathbf z\;\mathrm{d}\mathbf o\\
    =& \left(\sum_{\boldsymbol\beta_1+\boldsymbol\beta_2 = \beta}\binom{\boldsymbol\beta}{\boldsymbol\beta_1}\right)^2 \left(\max_{\boldsymbol\beta_2\leq \beta}\sup_{\mathbf x,\mathbf z,\mathbf o}\left|\partial^{\boldsymbol\alpha}_{\mathbf z}\partial^{\boldsymbol\beta_2}_{\mathbf o}p(\mathbf x\mid \mathbf z,\mathbf o)\right|^2\right) \max_{\boldsymbol\beta_1\leq \beta} \int_{\mathcal{O}}\int_{\mathcal{X}}\left(\partial^{\boldsymbol\beta_1}_{\mathbf o}w(\mathbf x,\mathbf o)\right)^2\;\mathrm{d}\mathbf x \;\mathrm{d}\mathbf o\\
    \stackrel{(d)}{=}& c_{m_o, d_o}\left(\max_{\boldsymbol\beta_2\leq \beta}\sup_{\mathbf x,\mathbf z,\mathbf o}\left|\partial^{\boldsymbol\alpha}_{\mathbf z}\partial^{\boldsymbol\beta_2}_{\mathbf o}p(\mathbf x\mid \mathbf z,\mathbf o)\right|^2\right)  \gamma_o^{-2|\beta|} \|w\|_{\mathcal{H}_{\gamma_x,\gamma_o}}^2\\
    \leq & c_{m_o,d_o} \left(\max_{\boldsymbol\alpha\leq m_z}\max_{\boldsymbol\beta\leq m_o}\sup_{\mathbf x,\mathbf z,\mathbf o}\left|\partial^{\boldsymbol\alpha}_{\mathbf z}\partial^{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\mathbf o}p(\mathbf x\mid \mathbf z,\mathbf o)\right|^2\right)  \gamma_o^{-2m_o} \|w\|_{\mathcal{H}_{\gamma_x,\gamma_o}}^2 ,
\end{align*}
\end{small}
where $(a)$ follows from the fact that, for any $f\in\mathcal{H}_{FO}$, there exists $w\in\mathcal{H}_{\gamma_x,\gamma_o}$ such that $f(\mathbf z,\mathbf o) = \langle w, F_{\ast}(\mathbf z,\mathbf o)\otimes\phi_{\gamma_o}(\mathbf o)\rangle_{\mathcal{H}_{\gamma_x,\gamma_o}} = \int_{\mathcal{X}}w(\mathbf x,\mathbf o)p(\mathbf x\mid \mathbf z,\mathbf o)\;\mathrm{d}\mathbf x$ and $\|f\|_{\mathcal{H}_{FO}} = \|w\|_{\mathcal{H}_{\gamma_x,\gamma_o}}$.
$(b)$ follows from generalized Leibniz's rule and differentiation under the integral sign \cite{klenke2013probability}[Theorem 6.28], $(c)$ follows from a Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.
$(d)$ follows from the following arguments.

From \citet[Theorem 4.21]{steinwart2008support}, we know that 
for any $w\in \mathcal{H}_{\gamma_x,\gamma_o}$, there exists $g\in L^2(\mathbb{R}^{d_x+d_o})$ such that 
\begin{align*}
    w(\mathbf x,\mathbf o) = \langle g, \Phi_{\gamma_x}(\mathbf x)\Phi_{\gamma_o}(\mathbf o)\rangle_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^{d_x+d_o})},\quad \|w\|_{\mathcal{H}_{\gamma_x,\gamma_o}} = \|g\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^{d_x+d_o})},
\end{align*}
with $\Phi_{\gamma_x}: \mathcal{X}\to L^2(\mathbb{R}^{d_x}), \Phi_{\gamma_o}: \mathcal{O}\to L^2(\mathbb{R}^{d_o})$ defined in \citet[Lemma 4.45]{steinwart2008support}.
We have
\begin{align*}
    &\int_{\mathcal{O}} \int_{\mathcal{X}}\left(\partial^{\boldsymbol\beta_1}_{\mathbf o}w(\mathbf x,\mathbf o)\right)^2\;\mathrm{d}\mathbf x \;\mathrm{d}\mathbf o\\
    =& \int_{\mathcal{O}}\int_{\mathcal{X}}\left(\partial_{\mathbf o}^{\boldsymbol\beta_1}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d_x+d_o}} g(\mathbf x',\mathbf o')\Phi_{\gamma_x}(\mathbf x)(\mathbf x')\Phi_{\gamma_o}(\mathbf o)(\mathbf o')\;\mathrm{d}\mathbf x'\;\mathrm{d}\mathbf o'\right)^{2}\;\mathrm{d}\mathbf x\;\mathrm{d}\mathbf o\\
    \stackrel{(i)}{=}& \int_{\mathcal{O}}\int_{\mathcal{X}}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d_x+d_o}} g(\mathbf x',\mathbf o')\Phi_{\gamma_x}(\mathbf x)(\mathbf x')\partial_{\mathbf o}^{\boldsymbol\beta_1}(\Phi_{\gamma_o}(\mathbf o)(\mathbf o'))\;\mathrm{d}\mathbf x'\;\mathrm{d}\mathbf o'\right)^{2}\;\mathrm{d}\mathbf x\;\mathrm{d}\mathbf o\\
    \leq &  \|g\|^2_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^{d_x+d_o})}\int_{\mathcal{O}}\int_{\mathcal{X}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d_x+d_o}} \left(\Phi_{\gamma_x}(\mathbf x)(\mathbf x')\partial_{\mathbf o}^{\boldsymbol\beta_1}(\Phi_{\gamma_o}(\mathbf o)(\mathbf o'))\right)^{2}\;\mathrm{d}\mathbf x'\;\mathrm{d}\mathbf o'\;\mathrm{d}\mathbf x\;\mathrm{d}\mathbf o\\
    = & \|g\|^2_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^{d_x+d_o})}\int_{\mathcal{O}}\int_{\mathcal{X}}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d_x}}(\Phi_{\gamma_x}(\mathbf x)(\mathbf x'))^2\;\mathrm{d}\mathbf x'\right) \left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d_o}}\left(\partial_{\mathbf o}^{\boldsymbol\beta_1}(\Phi_{\gamma_o}(\mathbf o)(\mathbf o'))\right)^{2}\;\mathrm{d}\mathbf o'\right)\;\mathrm{d}\mathbf x\;\mathrm{d}\mathbf o\\
    \stackrel{(ii)}{=} & \|g\|^2_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^{d_x+d_o})}\int_{\mathcal{O}} \int_{\mathbb{R}^{d_o}}\left(\partial_{\mathbf o}^{\boldsymbol\beta_1}(\Phi_{\gamma_o}(\mathbf o)(\mathbf o'))\right)^{2}\;\mathrm{d}\mathbf o'\;\mathrm{d}\mathbf o\\
    \stackrel{(iii)}{\leq} & \|g\|^2_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^{d_x+d_o})}c_{\boldsymbol\beta_1, d_o}\gamma_o^{-2|\boldsymbol\beta_1|} \\
    = & \|w\|^2_{\mathcal{H}_{\gamma_x,\gamma_o}} c_{\boldsymbol\beta_1, d_o}\gamma_o^{-2|\boldsymbol\beta_1|},
\end{align*}
where we're allowed to exchange differentiation and integration in $(i)$ using the differentiation lemma \cite{klenke2013probability}[Theorem 6.28], $(ii)$ follows from the fact that
\begin{align*}
    \int_{\mathbb{R}^{d_x}}(\Phi_{\gamma_x}(\mathbf x)(\mathbf x'))^2\;\mathrm{d}\mathbf x' = \int_{\mathbb{R}^{d_x}} \left(\frac{2^{d_x/2}}{\pi^{d_x/4}\gamma_x^{d_x/2}}\exp\left(-2\frac{\|\mathbf x - \mathbf x'\|^2_{2}}{\gamma_x^2}\right)\right)^2\;\mathrm{d}\mathbf x' = 1,
\end{align*}
and $(iii)$ follows from the proof of \cite{steinwart2008support}[Theorem 4.48]. Here $c_{\boldsymbol\beta_1,d_o}$ is a constant only depending on $\boldsymbol\beta_1,d_o$. Hence we've shown
\begin{align*}
    &\|f\|^2_{MW^{m_z,m_o}_2(\mathcal{Z}\times \mathcal{O};\mathbb{R})}\\
    = & \sum_{\boldsymbol\alpha\leq m_z, \boldsymbol\beta\leq m_o}\left\|\partial^{\boldsymbol\alpha}_{\mathbf z}\partial^{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\mathbf o}f\right\|^2_{L^2(\mathcal{Z}\times \mathcal{O};\mathbb{R})}\\
    \lesssim & \sum_{\boldsymbol\alpha \leq m_z, \boldsymbol\beta\leq m_o} \left(\max_{\boldsymbol\alpha\leq m_z}\max_{\boldsymbol\beta\leq m_o}\sup_{\mathbf x,\mathbf z,\mathbf o}\left|\partial^{\boldsymbol\alpha}_{\mathbf z}\partial^{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\mathbf o}p(\mathbf x\mid \mathbf z,\mathbf o)\right|^2\right)  \gamma_o^{-2m_o} \|w\|_{\mathcal{H}_{\gamma_x,\gamma_o}}^2\\
    = & \left(\sum_{\alpha \leq m_z, \boldsymbol\beta\leq m_o} 1\right) \left(\max_{\boldsymbol\alpha\leq m_z}\max_{\boldsymbol\beta\leq m_o}\sup_{\mathbf x,\mathbf z,\mathbf o}\left|\partial^{\boldsymbol\alpha}_{\mathbf z}\partial^{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\mathbf o}p(\mathbf x\mid \mathbf z,\mathbf o)\right|^2\right)  \gamma_o^{-2m_o} \|f\|_{\mathcal{H}_{FO}}^2 \\
    \lesssim &\rho^2 \gamma_o^{-2m_o} \|f\|_{\mathcal{H}_{FO}}^2 \\
    = & \rho^2 \gamma_o^{-2m_o} \|[f]\|_{[\mathcal{H}_{FO}]_{L^2(\mathcal{Z}\times \mathcal{O})}}^2 .
\end{align*}
The second last inequality holds by Assumption \ref{assn: technical}.
This concludes the proof.

\label{lem:embedintosobolevimplies}
Let $\mathcal{Z} = [0,1]^{d}$. Let $\mathcal{H}, W \subseteq L^2(\mathcal{Z})$ be two Hilbert spaces. Suppose that $\mathcal{H} \hookrightarrow W$ with embedding norm $\| \mathcal{H} \hookrightarrow W\| \leq c$. nodes.statement: We are going to apply citet[Theorem 3]JMLR:v25:23-1663 to obtain the desired result. To this end, we need to verify the assumptions (EVD) and (SRC) made in . Note that we let the assumption (EMB) of be trivially verified with alpha = 1, as we prove in Crefprop:F_ast_sobolev that F_ast in [G]^beta with beta > 1, therefore beta + p > 1 + p > 1 = alpha falls in Case 2 of Theorem 3 of . vspace3mm underlineVerification of (EVD) Let phi_Z (resp. phi_O) denote the feature map of H_Z (resp. H_O). Define C_ZO:H_Z otimes H_O to H_Z otimes H_O as the covariance operator. C_ZO = iint_ZtimesO (phi_Z(mathbf z) otimes phi_O(mathbf o)) otimes (phi_Z(mathbf z) otimes phi_O(mathbf o)) p_ZO(mathbf z, mathbf o) \;dmathbf z \;dmathbf o . We also define another two auxiliary covariance operators barC_Z:H_Zto H_Z and barC_O:H_Oto H_O. barC_Z = int_Z phi_Z(mathbf z) otimes phi_Z(mathbf z) p_ Z(mathbf z)\;dmathbf z, barC_O = int_O phi_O(mathbf o) otimes phi_O(mathbf o)p_O(mathbf o)\; dmathbf o . Since k_Z and k_O are bounded, C_ZO, barC_Z, barC_O are all self-adjoint compact operators. From and [Section 4], we have lambda_i(barC_Z) asymp i^-2 t_z/d_z and lambda_i(barC_O) asymp i^-2 t_o/d_o. We know from Assumption that P_ZO is equivalent to the Lebesgue measure, so by Jensen's inequality, we have C_ZO leq barC_Z otimes barC_O, where otimes here denotes an operator tensor product. Hence, from Lemma 17 of we have lambda_i(C_ZO) leq lambda_i(barC_Z otimes barC_O). Finally, from Creflem:tensor_evd we have lambda_i(C_ZO) leq lambda_i(barC_Z otimes barC_O) lesssim i^-2 t_z/d_z wedge 2 t_o/d_o + zeta for any zeta > 0. Therefore, we have proved that (EVD) hold with 1/p = 2 t_z/d_z wedge 2 t_o/d_o - zeta. Hence, p = d^dag/2 + zeta for any zeta > 0. vspace3mm underlineVerification of (SRC) Let beta = m^dag. By the definition of vector-valued interpolation space in [Definition 2] and the Assumption that P_ZO is equivalent to the Lebesgue measure, we have that [G]^beta &cong H_X,gamma_x otimes [L^2(ZtimesO), H_Z otimes H_O]_beta, 2 \\ &stackrel(a)cong H_X,gamma_x otimes [L^2(ZtimesO), W^t_z_2(Z) otimes W^t_o_2(O)]_beta, 2 \\ &stackrel(b)cong H_X,gamma_x otimes W^t_z beta_2(Z) otimes W^t_o beta_2(O)\\ &stackrel(ast)supseteq H_X,gamma_xotimes W^m_z_2(Z) otimes W^m_o_2(O)\\ &stackrel(c)cong H_X,gamma_xotimes MW^m_z,m_o_2(Ztimes O;R)\\ &stackrel(d)cong MW^m_z,m_o_2(Ztimes O;H_X,gamma_x). where in (a) we use Corollary 10.13 and Theorem 10.46 of , in (b) we use Creflem:tensor_interpolation, in (c) we use proposition 3.1 of , which shows MW^m_z, m_o_2(ZtimesO) cong W^m_z_2(Z) otimes W^m_o_2(O), and in (d) we use Creflem:vv_mss. Furthermore, the inclusion in (ast) is a continuous embedding. We show in Crefprop:F_ast_sobolev that under Crefassn: technical, \|F_ast\|_MW^m_z,m_o_2(Ztimes O;H_X,gamma_x) is bounded by a constant. Hence we deduce from the above embedding that F_astin [G]^beta, beta = m^dag = fracm_zt_z wedge fracm_ot_o. Hence \|F_ast\|_[G]^beta leq C for some constant C>0. Hence F_ast satisfies (SRC) in with beta=m^dag. Now we use Case 2 in Theorem 3 of to obtain the following result: if we take xi = tilden^-frac1m^dag + d^dag/2 + zeta, then for any 0leq gamma < m^dag, the following bound on the gamma-norm left\|left[hatF_xi -F_*right]right\|_gamma^2 leq tau^2 tilden^-fracm^dag - gammam^dag + d^dag/2 + zeta . holds with P^tilden-probability at least 1 - 4e^-tau. Therefore, noting that m^dag> 1, by taking gamma=0 and gamma=1, we obtain with P^tilden-probability at least 1 - 4e^-tau, left\|left[hatF_xi -F_*right]right\|_L^2(ZtimesO; H_X,gamma_x) leq tau tilden^-frac12fracm^dagm^dag + d^dag/2 + zeta , left\|hatF_xi -F_*right\|_G leq tau tilden^-frac12fracm^dag - 1m^dag + d^dag/2 + zeta .

Notice that, by definition of $F_{\ast}$, 
\begin{align*}
    \|F_{\ast}\|_{MW^{m_z, m_o}_2(\mathcal{Z}\times\mathcal{O};\mathcal{H}_{X,\gamma_x})} &= \left\|\int_{\mathcal{X}} \phi_{\gamma_x}(\mathbf x)p(\mathbf x|\cdot, \cdot)\;\mathrm{d} \mathbf x \right\|_{MW^{m_z, m_o}_2(\mathcal{Z}\times\mathcal{O};\mathcal{H}_{X,\gamma_x})} \\
    &\leq \int_{\mathcal{X}} \left\|\phi_{\gamma_x}(\mathbf x)p(\mathbf x|\cdot,\cdot )\right\|_{MW^{m_z, m_o}_2(\mathcal{Z}\times\mathcal{O};\mathcal{H}_{X,\gamma_x})}\;\mathrm{d} \mathbf x .
\end{align*}
In the last inequality above, we use \cite{Hytönen2016AnalysisBanachSpaces}[Proposition 1.2.11].
Next, notice that
\begin{align*}
    &\quad \left\|\phi_{\gamma_x}(\mathbf x) p(\mathbf x \mid \cdot,\cdot)\right\|_{MW^{m_z, m_o}_2(\mathcal{Z}\times\mathcal{O};\mathcal{H}_{X,\gamma_x})}^2 \\
    &= \sum_{|\boldsymbol\alpha|\leq m_z} \sum_{|\boldsymbol\beta|\leq m_o} \int_{\mathcal{Z}\times\mathcal{O}} \left\|\partial^{\boldsymbol\alpha}_\mathbf z \partial^{\boldsymbol\beta}_\mathbf o \left(\phi_{\gamma_x}(\mathbf x) p(\mathbf x\mid \mathbf z, \mathbf o) \right) \right\|_{\mathcal{H}_{X,\gamma_x}}^2 \;\mathrm{d} \mathbf z \;\mathrm{d} \mathbf o \\
    &= \sum_{|\boldsymbol\alpha|\leq m_z} \sum_{|\boldsymbol\beta|\leq m_o} \int_{\mathcal{Z}\times\mathcal{O}} \left\|\phi_{\gamma_x}(\mathbf x) \partial^{\boldsymbol\alpha}_\mathbf z \partial^{\boldsymbol\beta}_\mathbf o p(\mathbf x \mid \mathbf z, \mathbf o) \right\|_{\mathcal{H}_{X,\gamma_x}}^2 \;\mathrm{d} \mathbf z \;\mathrm{d} \mathbf o \\
    &\leq \sum_{|\boldsymbol\alpha|\leq m_z} \sum_{|\boldsymbol\beta|\leq m_o} \int_{\mathcal{Z}\times \mathcal{O}} \left|\partial^{\boldsymbol\alpha}_\mathbf z \partial^{\boldsymbol\beta}_\mathbf o p(\mathbf x| \mathbf z, \mathbf o) \right|^2 \;\mathrm{d} \mathbf z \;\mathrm{d} \mathbf o \\ 
    &\leq \binom{m_z + d_z -1}{d_z -1} \binom{m_o + d_o-1}{d_o -1} \rho^2  .
\end{align*}
In the last step, $\binom{m_z + d_z -1}{d_z -1}$ shows up as the evaluation of $\sum_{|\boldsymbol\alpha| \leq m_z} 1$.

    \begin{align*}
        &\quad \lambda \|\bar{f}_{\lambda}\|^2_{\mathcal{H}_{XO}} \\
        &\stackrel{(a)}{\leq} C_1\hat{\rho}\left(\lambda \|f_{\lambda}\|^2_{\mathcal{H}_{XO}} + \|T(f_{\lambda} - f_{\ast})\|^2_{L^2(P_{ZO})} + M_n^{2+2p}\left(\frac{\max\{4, \tilde{c}_p\}^{2p}\gamma_x^{-d_x}\gamma_o^{-d_o}}{\lambda^{p}n}\right) + \frac{M_n^2}{n}\right)\\
        &\stackrel{(b)}{\leq}  C_2\hat{\rho}\left(n^{-\frac{2(\frac{s_x}{d_x}+\eta_1)}{1+(2+\frac{d_o}{s_o})(\frac{s_x}{d_x}+\eta_1)}} + M_n^{2+2p}\left(\frac{\max\{4, \tilde{c}_p\}^{2p}\gamma_x^{-d_x}\gamma_o^{-d_o}}{\lambda^{p}n}\right) + \frac{M_n^2}{n}\right)\\

By definition of f_lambda, we have & lambda \| f_lambda\|_H_gamma_x,gamma_o^2 + left\|Tleft(f_ast - left[f_lambdaright]right)right\|_L^2(P_ZO)^2 nonumber \\ &=inf_fin H_gamma_x,gamma_olambda \|f\|_H_gamma_x,gamma_o^2 + left\|Tf_ast - T[f]right\|_L^2(P_ZO)^2nonumber \\ &leq lambda \|f_aux\|_H_gamma_x,gamma_o^2 + left\|Tf_ast - T[f_aux]right\|_L^2(P_ZO)^2 nonumber \\ &leq lambda \|f_aux \|_H_gamma_x,gamma_o^2 + left\|Tf_ast - T left(f_ast ast K_gamma_o right)right\|_L^2(P_ZO)^2 nonumber \\ &+left\| Tleft((f_ast - f_ast , low) ast K_gamma_o - (f_ast - f_ast, low) ast K_gamma_o ast K_gamma_xright) right\|_L^2(P_ZO)^2. For the first term, we know from Eq.~ and Crefass:f_ast in the main text that lambda\|f_aux\|_H_gamma_x,gamma_o^2 leq n^-1 cdot 2 n^frac1+fracd_os_o(fracs_xd_x+eta_1)1+(2+fracd_os_o)(fracs_xd_x+eta_1) \|f_ast\|_L^2(R^d_x+d_o) leq 2 n^-frac2(fracs_xd_x+eta_1)1+(2+fracd_os_o)(fracs_xd_x+eta_1) . For the second term, we have left\|Tf_ast - T left(f_ast ast K_gamma_o right)right\|_L^2(P_ZO)^2 &leq left\|f_ast - f_ast ast K_gamma_o right\|_L^2(P_XO)^2 \\ &lesssim left\|f_ast - f_ast ast K_gamma_o right\|_L^2(XtimesO)^2 \\ &lesssim |f_ast|^2_B^s_x,s_o_2,q(R^d_x+d_o) cdot max\0, gamma_o^2s_o\\\ &= |f_ast|^2_B^s_x,s_o_2,q(R^d_x+d_o) n^-frac2(fracs_xd_x+eta_1)1+(2+fracd_os_o)(fracs_xd_x+eta_1). The first inequality above holds because T is a bounded operator; the second inequality holds by Assumption that P_XO admits a bounded density. The second last inequality above holds by using Creflem:hang_prop_3 for boldsymbolgamma = (underbrace0,dots, 0_d_x,underbracegamma_o,dots,gamma_o_d_o). For the third term, we note that (forall mathbf oin R^d_o), F[left((f_ast - f_ast , low) ast K_gamma_o - (f_ast - f_ast, low) ast K_gamma_o ast K_gamma_xright)(cdot, mathbf o)] is supported on the complement of \mathbf x: \|mathbf x\| leq gamma_x^-1\ (see~Eq. ). Thus it follows from Crefass:T_contractivity that & left\| Tleft((f_ast - f_ast , low) ast K_gamma_o - (f_ast - f_ast, low) ast K_gamma_o ast K_gamma_xright) right\|_L^2(P_ZO)^2 \\ &leq gamma_x^2d_xeta_1left\| (f_ast - f_ast , low) ast K_gamma_o - (f_ast - f_ast, low) ast K_gamma_o ast K_gamma_x right\|_L^2(P_XO)^2\\ &stackrel(i)lesssim gamma_x^2d_xeta_1+ 2s_xcdot left|(f_ast - f_ast , low) ast K_gamma_oright|^2_B^s_x,s_o_2,q(R^d_x+d_o)\\ &stackrel(ii)leq gamma_x^2d_xeta_1+ 2s_xcdot left|f_ast ast K_gamma_oright|^2_B^s_x,s_o_2,q(R^d_x+d_o)\\ &stackrel(iii)leq gamma_x^2d_xeta_1+ 2s_xcdot left|f_astright|^2_B^s_x,s_o_2,q(R^d_x+d_o) \|K_gamma_o\|^2_L^1(R^d_o)\\ &stackrel(iv)lesssim n^-frac2(fracs_xd_x+eta_1)1+(2+fracd_os_o)(fracs_xd_x+eta_1). In the above derivations, (i) follows by using Creflem:hang_prop_3 for boldsymbolgamma = (underbracegamma_x,dots,gamma_x_d_x,underbrace0,dots,0_d_o) and the Assumption that P_XO admits a bounded density, (ii) follows from the proof of Creflem:new_besov_mask, (iii) follows from Creflem:besov_young, and (iv) follows by the fact that \|K_gamma_o\|_L^1(R)= 1 citep[Section 4.1.2]Giné_Nickl_2015 and Crefass:f_ast in the main text. Combine the upper bound on the three terms in Eq.~ and we obtain lambda \| f_lambda\|_H_gamma_x,gamma_o^2 + left\|Tleft(f_ast - left[f_lambdaright]right)right\|_L^2(P_ZO)^2 leq n^-frac2(fracs_xd_x+eta_1)1+(2+fracd_os_o)(fracs_xd_x+eta_1). Then fin L^2(Omega_1, W^p(Omega_2,H)) such that partial_1^alphafin L^2(Omega_1, W^p(Omega_2,H)) for |alpha|leq m. As explained in [Definition 2.5.1], to say that partial_1^alphafin L^2(Omega_1, W^p(Omega_2,H)) is equivalent to saying that for every phi in C^infty_c(Omega_1), we have int_Omega_1f(x,cdot)partial^alpha_1phi(x)\;dx = (-1)^|alpha|int_Omega_1(partial^alpha_1f)(x,cdot)phi(x)\;dx belongs to W^p(Omega_2,H). Suppose $\left( \mu_{1, i} \right)_{i \in \mathbb{N}^+}$ (resp. $\left( \mu_{2, j} \right)_{j \in \mathbb{N}^+}$) are the eigenvalues of $\Sigma_1$ (resp. $\Sigma_2$) with corresponding eigenfunctions $\left( q_{1, i} \right)_{i \in \mathbb{N}^+}$ (resp. $\left( q_{2, j} \right)_{j \in \mathbb{N}^+}$). 
By definition of operator tensor product, we have
\begin{align*}
    \left( \Sigma_1 \otimes \Sigma_2 \right) (q_{1, i} \otimes q_{2, j} ) = \left( \Sigma_1  q_{1, i} \right) \otimes \left( \Sigma_2 q_{2, j} \right) = \mu_{1, i} \mu_{2, j} (q_{1, i} \otimes q_{2, j} ) .
\end{align*}
Therefore, for any $i \in \mathbb{N}^+, j \in \mathbb{N}^+$ we obtain that $\mu_{1, i} \cdot \mu_{2, j}$ is the eigenvalue of $\Sigma_1 \otimes_{op} \Sigma_2$ with corresponding eigenfunction $q_{1, i} \otimes q_{2, j}$. 
Therefore the eigenvalues of $\Sigma_1 \otimes_{op} \Sigma_2$ equal the tensor product of two sequences $(\mu_{1, i})_{i\in \mathbb{N}^+}$ and $(\mu_{2, j})_{j \in \mathbb{N}^+}$. 

Without loss of generality, we assume $p_1 \leq p_2$ so that $\mu_{1, i} \leq \mu_{2, i}$ for $i$ large enough. 
Denote $(\sigma_n)_{n\in \mathbb{N}^+}$ as the tensor product of two sequences $(\mu_{2, i})_{i\in \mathbb{N}^+}$ and $(\mu_{2, j})_{j \in \mathbb{N}^+}$ rearranged in a non-increasing order. Hence, we have $\lambda_{n}(\Sigma_1 \otimes \Sigma_2) \leq \sigma_n$.
From \cite{krieg2018tensor}, we have 
\begin{align*}
    \sigma_n \leq n^{- 1/p_2} (\log n)^{1/p_2} \leq n^{- 1/p_2 + \zeta},
\end{align*}
for any $\zeta > 0$.
It concludes the proof.

Following the same arguments in the proof of proposition 4 in \cite{hang2021optimal}, we have $ K_{\boldsymbol{\gamma}} \ast f \in \mathcal{H}_{X,\boldsymbol{\gamma}}$.
For a function $f:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}$, we define $\tau_{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}f(\mathbf x) = f(\boldsymbol{\gamma}\odot \mathbf x)$. We have, for all $\mathbf x \in \mathbb{R}^d$, 
\begin{align*}
    \tau_{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}\left(K_{\boldsymbol{\gamma}} \ast f\right)(\mathbf x) &= \int_{\mathbb{R}^d}K_{\boldsymbol{\gamma}} \left( \boldsymbol{\gamma} \odot \mathbf x - \boldsymbol{t} \right) f(\boldsymbol{t}) \;\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{t} \\
    &=  \int_{\mathbb{R}^d}K_{\mathbf{1}}\left(\frac{\boldsymbol{\gamma} \odot \mathbf x - \boldsymbol{t}}{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}\right)\left(\prod_{i=1}^{d}\frac{1}{\gamma_i} \right)f(\boldsymbol{t})\;\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{t}\\
    &= \int_{\mathbb{R}^d}K_{\mathbf{1}}\left(\mathbf x - \frac{\boldsymbol{t}}{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}\right)\left(\prod_{i=1}^{d}\frac{1}{\gamma_i} \right)f\left( \boldsymbol{t} \right)\;\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{t}\\
    &= \int_{\mathbb{R}^d}K_{\mathbf{1}}\left(\mathbf x - \boldsymbol{t}\right)f\left(\boldsymbol{t} \odot\boldsymbol{\gamma}\right)\;\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{t}\\
    &= (K_{\mathbf{1}}\ast (\tau_{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}f))(\mathbf x) .
\end{align*}
Proposition 4.37 of \cite{steinwart2008support} can be generalized to anisotropic case which shows that for any  
$f \in \mathcal{H}_{X,\boldsymbol{\gamma}}$, $\tau_{\boldsymbol{\gamma}} f \in \mathcal{H}_{X, \mathbf{1}}$ and 
$\tau_{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}: \mathcal{H}_{X,\boldsymbol{\gamma}} \to \mathcal{H}_{X, \mathbf{1}}$ is an isometric isomorphism.  Hence we have
\begin{align*}
    \left\|K_{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}\ast f \right\|_{\mathcal{H}_{X,\boldsymbol{\gamma}}} &= \left\|\tau_{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}\left(K_{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}\ast f\right) \right\|_{\mathcal{H}_{X, \mathbf{1}}}\\
    &= \left\|K_{\mathbf{1}}\ast (\tau_{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}f)\right\|_{\mathcal{H}_{X, \mathbf{1}}}\\
    &\leq \pi^{-\frac{d}{4}}(2^r - 1) \|\tau_{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}f\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^d)}\\
    &= \left(\prod_{i=1}^{d}\gamma_i^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right)\pi^{-\frac{d}{4}}(2^r - 1)\|f\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^d)},
\end{align*}
where the second last inequality follows from \cite{eberts2013optimal}[Theorem 2.3] setting $\gamma=1$.

nodes.statement: In contrast to the notation used in the rest of the document (with the exception of Creflem:l2toprojected_illp), in this proof, we use F to denote the unitary Fourier operator on L^2(R^d_x+d_o), we use F_x to denote the unitary Fourier operator on L^2(R^d_x), and we use F_o to denote the unitary Fourier operator on L^2(R^d_o). We let otimes: L^2(R^d_x)times L^2(R^d_o)to L^2(R^d_x+d_o) denotes the tensor product mapping, where (fotimes g)(mathbf x,mathbf o) = f(mathbf x)g(mathbf o) for all (mathbf x,mathbf o)in R^d_x+d_o. By considering a convergent sequence to f_1 in L^1(R^d_x)cap L^2(R^d_x), and similarly for f_2, we can show that F[fotimes g] = F_x[f]otimes F_o[g] for fin L^2(R^d_x) and gin L^2(R^d_o). At the start of Crefsec:proof_upper, we proved that for fin L^1(R^d_x+d_o), fast F^-1[iota_x,gamma_x^-1] in L^2(R^d_x+d_o). Since \|K_gamma_o\|_L^1(R^d_o)= 1 citep[Section 4.1.2]Giné_Nickl_2015, we have \|(fast F^-1[iota_x,gamma_x^-1])ast K_gamma_o\|_L^2(R^d_x+d_o)^2 &stackrel(a)= int_R^d_x\|(fast F^-1[iota_x,gamma_x^-1])(mathbf x,cdot) ast K_gamma_o\|^2_L^2(R^d_o)\;dmathbf x\\ &stackrel(b)leq int_R^d_x \|(fast F^-1[iota_x,gamma_x^-1])(mathbf x,cdot)\|^2_L^2(R^d_o) \|K_gamma_o\|^2_L^1(R^d_o)\\ & = \|fast F^-1[iota_x,gamma_x^-1]\|^2_L^2(R^d_x+d_o). where in (a), (fast F^-1[iota_x,gamma_x^-1])(mathbf x,cdot) is a slice function of any representative of fast F^-1[iota_x,gamma_x^-1]in L^2(R^d_x), and (b) follows from Young's Convolution Inequality. Hence we can apply F to fast F^-1[iota_x,gamma_x^-1]in L^2(R^d_x+d_o) and we find Fleft[F_x^-1[iota_x,gamma_x^-1] ast K_gamma_o ast fright] = (iota_x,gamma_x^-1otimes F_o[K_gamma_o]) cdot F[f]. For phi(mathbf x,mathbf o) = exp(- gamma_x^-2 \|mathbf x\|_2^2) cdot exp(- gamma_o^-2 \|mathbf o\|_2^2), its Fourier transform is F[phi](boldsymbolomega_x,boldsymbolomega_o) = pi^d_x/2+d_o/2 gamma_x^d_x expleft(-frac14 gamma_x^2 \|boldsymbolomega_x\|_2^2right) cdot gamma_o^d_oexpleft(-frac14 gamma_o^2 \|boldsymbolomega_o\|_2^2right). Hence, by definition of Gaussian RKHS norm~citep[Theorem 10.12]wendland2004scattered, & left\| F_x^-1[iota_x,gamma_x^-1]ast K_gamma_o ast fright\|_H_gamma_x,gamma_o^2 \\ &= int_R^d_x+d_o fracleft(iota_x,gamma_x^-1(boldsymbolomega_x) cdot F[f](boldsymbolomega_x,boldsymbolomega_o) cdot F_o[K_gamma_o](boldsymbolomega_o)right)^2pi^d_x/2+d_o/2 gamma_x^d_x expleft(-frac14 gamma_x^2 \|boldsymbolomega_x\|_2^2right) cdot gamma_o^d_oexp(-frac14 gamma_o^2 \|boldsymbolomega_o\|_2^2) \;dboldsymbolomega_x \;dboldsymbolomega_o \\ &lesssim gamma_x^-d_x gamma_o^-d_o int_R^d_oint_\boldsymbolomega_x: \|boldsymbolomega_x\|_2 leq gamma_x^-1 \ fracleft( F[f](boldsymbolomega_x,boldsymbolomega_o) cdot F_o[K_gamma_o](boldsymbolomega_o)right)^2expleft(-frac14 gamma_x^2 \|boldsymbolomega_x\|_2^2right) cdot exp(-frac14 gamma_o^2 \|boldsymbolomega_o\|_2^2) \;dboldsymbolomega_x \;dboldsymbolomega_o \\ &lesssim gamma_x^-d_x gamma_o^-d_o int_R^d_x+d_o expleft(frac14 gamma_o^2 \|boldsymbolomega_o\|_2^2right)left(F[f](boldsymbolomega_x,boldsymbolomega_o) cdot F_o[K_gamma_o](boldsymbolomega_o)right)^2 \;dboldsymbolomega_x \;dboldsymbolomega_o . Since K_gamma_o(mathbf o) := sum_j=1^rbinomrj(-1)^1-j frac1j^d_ogamma_o^d_oleft(frac2piright)^fracd2 exp( -2 j^-2 gamma_o^-2 \|mathbf o\|_2^2), so we have F_o[K_gamma_o](boldsymbolomega_o) = sum_j=1^rbinomrj(-1)^1-j expleft(-frac18 j^2 gamma_o^2 \|boldsymbolomega_o\|_2^2right) . Consequently, we have & left\| F^-1[iota_x,gamma_x^-1]ast K_gamma_o ast fright\|_H_gamma_x,gamma_o^2 \\ &lesssim gamma_x^-d_x gamma_o^-d_o int_R^d_x+d_o fracleft(F[f](boldsymbolomega_x,boldsymbolomega_o) cdot sum_j=1^rbinomrj(-1)^1-j exp(-frac18 j^2 gamma_o^2 \|boldsymbolomega_o\|_2^2) right)^2exp(-frac14 gamma_o^2 \|boldsymbolomega_o\|_2^2) dboldsymbolomega_x dboldsymbolomega_o \\ &leq gamma_x^-d_x gamma_o^-d_o 2^2r int_R^d_x+d_o left(F[f](boldsymbolomega_x,boldsymbolomega_o) right)^2 dboldsymbolomega_x dboldsymbolomega_o \\ &= gamma_x^-d_x gamma_o^-d_o 2^2r \| f\|_L^2(R^d_x+d_o)^2 . where the last equality follows by Plancherel's Theorem.

Note that tildeIsubset I. Let iota_x : R^d_xto \0,1\ denote the indicator function on I_mathbf x, let iota_o : R^d_oto \0,1\ denote the indicator function on I_mathbf o, let iota: R^d_x+d_oto \0,1\ denote the indicator function on I, which satisfies iota = iota_x cdot iota_o. Thus we have & \|f\|_L^2(P_XO) nonumber \\ &leq left\|fast F^-1(iota)right\|_L^2(P_XO) + left\|fast F^-1(iota) - fright\|_L^2(P_XO) nonumber \\ &stackrel(i)leq gamma_x^-d_xeta_0 (log (gamma_x^-delta_x))^fracd_xeta_02 \|T(fast F^-1(iota))\|_L^2(P_ZO) + left\|fast F^-1(iota) - fright\|_L^2(P_XO) nonumber\\ &stackrel(ii)leq gamma_x^-d_xeta_0 (log (gamma_x^-delta_x))^fracd_xeta_02 \|Tf\|_L^2(P_ZO) nonumber \\ & + left(1 + gamma_x^-d_xeta_0 (log (gamma_x^-delta_x))^fracd_xeta_02 right)left\|fast F^-1(iota) - fright\|_L^2(P_XO) nonumber \\ &lesssim gamma_x^-d_xeta_0 (log (gamma_x^-delta_x))^fracd_xeta_02 \|Tf\|_L^2(P_ZO) + gamma_x^-d_xeta_0 (log (gamma_x^-delta_x))^fracd_xeta_02 left\|fast F^-1(iota) - fright\|_L^2(XtimesO) . In the above derivations, item (i) follows from Crefass:T_frequency_ill_posedness, and for F_x,F_o defined in the proof of Creflem:mixed_convolution, (forall mathbf oin O),\; supp(F_x[(fast F^-1(iota))(cdot,mathbf o)]) = supp(F_x[(fast F_o^-1[iota_o])(cdot, mathbf o)] cdot iota_x) subseteq I_mathbf x, where we note that the relevant Fourier transforms exist since fin H_gamma_x,gamma_osubset L^2(R^d_x+d_o). item (ii) follows from a triangular inequality and a Jensen's inequality. Next, we bound (ast) =\|fast F^-1(iota) - f\|_L^2([0,1]^d_x+d_o). We have (ast) &= left\|fast F^-1(iota) - fright\|_L^2([0,1]^d_x+d_o) leq left\|fast F^-1(iota) - fright\|_L^2(R^d_x+d_o)\\ &stackrel(a)= left\|Fleft[fast F^-1(iota) - fright]right\|_L^2(R^d_x+d_o)= \|F[f]iota - F[f]\|_L^2(R^d_x+d_o)\\ &= left(int_I^c |F[f](boldsymbolomega)|^2\;dboldsymbolomegaright)^frac12 stackrel(b)leq left(int_tildeI^c |F[f](boldsymbolomega)|^2\;dboldsymbolomegaright)^frac12 , where (a) holds by Plancherel's Theorem, (b) holds by tildeIsubseteq I. Recall that for a, binR^d, a odot b := (a_1 b_1, ldots, a_d b_d) in R^d. For boldsymbolomega=(boldsymbolomega_x, boldsymbolomega_o), we proceed from above to have, &leq left(int_tildeI^c |F[f](boldsymbolomega)|^2 expleft(frac\|(boldsymbolomega_x odot boldsymbolgamma_x, boldsymbolomega_o odot boldsymbolgamma_o )\|^2_24right)expleft(-frac\|(boldsymbolomega_x odot boldsymbolgamma_x, boldsymbolomega_o odot boldsymbolgamma_o ) \|^2_24right)\;dboldsymbolomegaright)^frac12\\ &leq sup_boldsymbolomegain tildeI^cexpleft(-frac\|(boldsymbolomega_x odot boldsymbolgamma_x, boldsymbolomega_o odot boldsymbolgamma_o )\|^2_28right)left(int_R^d_x+d_o |F[f](boldsymbolomega)|^2 expleft(frac\|(boldsymbolomega_x odot boldsymbolgamma_x, boldsymbolomega_o odot boldsymbolgamma_o ) \|^2_24right)\;dboldsymbolomegaright)^frac12\\ &stackrel(c)leq sup_boldsymbolomegain tildeI^cexpleft(-frac\|(boldsymbolomega_x odot boldsymbolgamma_x, boldsymbolomega_o odot boldsymbolgamma_o ) \|^2_28right)left( \|f\|_H_XO,boldsymbolgamma_x,boldsymbolgamma_o^2 2^-fracd_x+d_o2 gamma_x^d_xgamma_o^d_oright)^frac12\\ &lesssim sup_\|boldsymbolomega_x\|_2^2 gamma_x^2 (log (gamma_x^-delta_x))^-1 + \|boldsymbolomega_o\|^2gamma_o^2 (log (gamma_o^-delta_o))^-1 geq 1 expleft(-frac gamma_x^2 \|boldsymbolomega_x\|_2^2 + gamma_o^2 \|boldsymbolomega_o\|_2^2 8right)left(n gamma_x^d_xgamma_o^d_oright)^frac12 \\ &leq expleft(-frac18 log(gamma_x^-delta_x ) right)left(n gamma_x^d_x gamma_o^d_oright)^frac12 \\ &asymp gamma_x^frac18 delta_x left(n gamma_x^d_xgamma_o^d_o right)^1/2, where (c) holds by Lemma~. Now we have proved the first claim of this lemma. Next, we proceed to prove the second claim by plugging in the specific values of delta_x,delta_o and gamma_x,gamma_o. Recall that frac18 delta_x = 2s_x + d_xeta_1 + d_x eta_0 + d_x, we obtain (ast) lesssim n^-fracfracdelta_x8frac1d_x1+(2+fracd_os_o)(fracs_xd_x+eta_1) cdot n^fracfracs_xd_x+eta_11+(2+fracd_os_o)(fracs_xd_x+eta_1) = n^frac-fracs_xd_x - eta_0 - 11+(2+fracd_os_o)(fracs_xd_x+eta_1) . By definition of the operator norm, we have
\begin{align*}
    &\quad \|C_{FO}\|^2 \\
    &= \sup_{\|f\|_{\mathcal{H}_{\gamma_x,\gamma_o}} = 1}\left\langle f, \mathbb{E}[(F_{\ast}(Z, O) \otimes \phi_{\gamma_o}(O))\otimes (F_{\ast}(Z, O) \otimes \phi_{\gamma_o}(O))]f\right\rangle_{\mathcal{H}_{\gamma_x,\gamma_o}}\\ 
    =& \sup_{\|f\|_{\mathcal{H}_{\gamma_x,\gamma_o}} = 1} \mathbb{E} \left[ \left(\mathbb{E}[f(X,O)|Z,O] \right)^2 \right]\\
    \geq & \sup_{\|f\|_{\mathcal{H}_{\gamma_x,\gamma_o}} = 1} \left( \mathbb{E}_{ZO \sim P_{ZO}} \left[\mathbb{E}[f(X,O)|Z,O]\right] \right)^2\\
    =&  \sup_{\|f\|_{\mathcal{H}_{\gamma_x,\gamma_o}} = 1} \mathbb{E}[f(X,O)]^2 \\
    =& \|\mu_{XO}\|_{\mathcal{H}_{\gamma_x,\gamma_o}}^2 , 
\end{align*}
where $\mu_{XO} := \mathbb{E}_{P_{XO}}[\phi_{\gamma_x}(X) \otimes \phi_{\gamma_o}(O)]$. 
Notice that 
\begin{align*}
    &\|\mu_{XO} \|_{\mathcal{H}_{\gamma_x,\gamma_o}}^2\\ &= \left\langle \iint_{\mathcal{O}\times\mathcal{X}} \phi_{\gamma_x}(\mathbf x) \otimes \phi_{\gamma_o}(\mathbf o) p_{XO}(\mathbf x,\mathbf o)\;\mathrm{d}\mathbf x \;\mathrm{d}\mathbf o, \right. \\
    &\qquad\qquad \left. \iint_{\mathcal{O}\times\mathcal{X}} \phi_{\gamma_x}(\mathbf x') \otimes \phi_{\gamma_o}(\mathbf o') p_{XO}(\mathbf x',\mathbf o')\;\mathrm{d}\mathbf x'\;\mathrm{d}\mathbf o'\right\rangle_{\mathcal{H}_{\gamma_x,\gamma_o}}\\
    &= \iint_{\mathcal{O}\times\mathcal{X}} \iint_{\mathcal{O}\times\mathcal{X}} K_{\gamma_o}(\mathbf o,\mathbf o') K_{\gamma_x}(\mathbf x,\mathbf x')p_{XO}(\mathbf x,\mathbf o) p_{XO}(\mathbf x', \mathbf o')\;\mathrm{d}\mathbf x\;\mathrm{d}\mathbf x'\;\mathrm{d}\mathbf o\;\mathrm{d}\mathbf o'\\
    &\stackrel{(a)}{\geq} a^2\int_{[1/4,3/4]^{d_o}}\int_{[1/4,3/4]^{d_o}} K_{\gamma_o}(\mathbf o,\mathbf o')\;\mathrm{d}\mathbf o\;\mathrm{d}\mathbf o'\int_{[1/4,3/4]^{d_x}}\int_{[1/4,3/4]^{d_x}} K_{\gamma_x}(\mathbf x,\mathbf x') \;\mathrm{d}\mathbf x\;\mathrm{d}\mathbf x'\\
    &\stackrel{(b)} = a^2 \left(\gamma_x \sqrt{\pi} \left[\frac{\mathrm{erf}\left(\frac{1}{2\gamma_x}\right)}{2} + \gamma_x\frac{\exp\left(-\frac{1}{4\gamma_x^2}\right)-1}{\sqrt{\pi}}\right]\right)^{d_x} \\
    &\qquad\qquad \cdot \left(\gamma_o \sqrt{\pi} \left[\frac{\mathrm{erf}\left(\frac{1}{2\gamma_o}\right)}{2} + \gamma_o\frac{\exp\left(-\frac{1}{4\gamma_o^2}\right)-1}{\sqrt{\pi}}\right]\right)^{d_o},
\end{align*}
where $\mathrm{erf}(x) := \frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}}\int^{x}_{-x}\exp\left(-t^2\right)\;\mathrm{d}t$
is the standard error function of normal distribution. Step $(a)$ holds by \Cref{assn: technical} and step $(b)$ holds by using \Cref{lem:gaussian_kernel_embedding}. We plug in $\gamma_x = n^{-\frac{\frac{1}{d_x}}{1+(2+\frac{d_o}{s_o})(\frac{s_x}{d_x}+\eta_1)}}$, $\gamma_o = n^{-\frac{\frac{1}{s_o}(\frac{s_x}{d_x}+\eta_1)}{1+(2+\frac{d_o}{s_o})(\frac{s_x}{d_x}+\eta_1)}}$ to obtain
\begin{align*}
    \|\mu_{XO}\|^2_{\mathcal{H}_{\gamma_x,\gamma_o}} &\stackrel{(i)}{\geq} a^2\left(\sqrt{\pi}\gamma_x/4\right)^{d_x}\left(\sqrt{\pi}\gamma_o/4\right)^{d_o} = a^2 (\sqrt{\pi}/4)^{d_x+d_o} n^{-\frac{1+\frac{d_o}{s_o}(\frac{s_x}{d_x}+\eta_1)}{1+(2+\frac{d_o}{s_o})(\frac{s_x}{d_x}+\eta_1)}},
\end{align*}
where $(i)$ holds for sufficiently large $n\geq 1$ because $\mathrm{erf}(x)\geq \frac{1}{2}$ when $x\geq 1$.
